issues.explanation: 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically to the rest of this rape-related profile. The other triggers, threats, appraisals, and strategies center on interpersonal closeness, malevolent intent, bodily vulnerability, and interpersonal hypervigilance; cycling stands out as a highly specific cue without support elsewhere in the formulation.

The profile otherwise centers on interpersonal/sexual threat and hypervigilance, so this appraisal appears disconnected from the formulation.

vignette:
Marisol had spent much of her adult life working as an environmental scientist, a role that took her into field stations, remote sites, and long stretches of solitary travel across the American West. Even now, at 77, she still described herself as someone who had always been comfortable in practical settings and uneasy with sentimentality, a woman who preferred checklists to small talk. That changed after a rape in midlife, an assault that she recalled in fragmented, vivid pieces: the sudden realization that she was alone with a man she had not expected to be dangerous, the force of the violation, and the humiliating awareness of what had been done to her body. In the years that followed, Marisol found herself thinking back over the event again and again, turning it over in her mind as if some overlooked detail might explain how it had happened or how it could have been stopped. She had come to believe that the assault happened because of the way she acted, scrutinizing her own choices with a harsh, self-directed certainty, and she also carried a deep sense of shame about what had happened to her body.

What startled her most in the months after the assault were the ordinary moments that suddenly felt loaded with danger. A friendly hug from a colleague, a hand on her shoulder from an acquaintance, or even being expected to stand close during a social greeting could make her stiffen before she could stop herself. Sexual situations, even when they were only implied in conversation or portrayed on television, became intolerable; she would turn away, change the channel, or leave the room before the feeling of being exposed became too much. Being alone with men became especially difficult. If a repairman, neighbor, or former coworker came by, she arranged to keep a door open, to have a second person present, or to end the interaction as quickly as possible. She did not describe these choices as dramatic, only necessary, as if caution had become the price of getting through the day.

Marisol’s world gradually narrowed around the need to feel prepared. Before entering a restaurant, clinic, or unfamiliar office, she automatically looked for exits and positioned herself so she could leave quickly if needed. Open parking lots, broad sidewalks, and exposed outdoor spaces made her feel uncomfortably visible, and she found herself choosing routes and destinations that offered walls, corners, or some kind of shelter. At work, when she was still traveling for environmental assessments, she preferred sites where she could stay near a vehicle or a building entrance, and even in retirement she noticed the same reflex in community gardens, museums, and public parks. She would scan the layout before settling in, identifying escape routes before she could relax. In the same way, she became watchful for sudden movements from others; a person turning too quickly toward her, stepping in from the side, or reaching unexpectedly could leave her on guard in an instant. She did not feel able to dismiss these reactions, because in her mind the world had become a place where harm could come from someone no one would suspect.

At home, the feeling of vulnerability did not leave her at the door. Marisol listened carefully for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home, especially at night, and she found herself attentive to every creak, footstep, or change in the usual rhythm of the house. That vigilance left her tired, but she said she could not afford not to do it. Her attention was also pulled backward into repetitive thoughts about how the assault could have been prevented, and she often found herself replaying decisions from that period in exacting detail, as though the answer were hidden in her own memory. These private reviews were accompanied by a long-standing sense that other people might be capable of harm without warning, a conviction that made even routine trust feel precarious.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was no longer only trying to manage one painful memory; she was trying to make sense of a life that had been organized around avoiding reminders of it. She had begun declining invitations that involved close contact, worrying that a hug or a moment of intimacy would bring back the assault in a way she could not control. Her avoidance of eye contact with other people had also become more noticeable, especially in settings where men were present, because meeting someone’s gaze made her feel exposed and readable in a way she disliked. Although she remained independent and continued to manage her affairs, she described herself as living with constant tension, always braced, always calculating where she could move if she needed to leave. She came to treatment because she was weary of feeling hunted by ordinary spaces and ordinary interactions, and because at this stage of life she wanted, more than anything, to be able to sit in a room, hear a footstep, accept a greeting, or walk across an open place without instantly feeling that danger was already on its way.
